title: Growth Will Cost You Things That Used to Feel Safe
author: Summer Mulder
summary: Mulder starts with a recognisable sensation, leaving a conversation feeling less like yourself after holding back a win, playing down a goal or laughing at something that was not funny. She argues this is a predictable side effect of growth: coming into alignment with who you are now brings quiet grief rather than dramatic ruptures, showing up as fewer texts, more tension and a hard-to-name sense of misalignment, followed by guilt. Her central claim is that you cannot grow and pretend at the same time, because at some point the effort of maintaining the version of you someone else prefers exceeds what you have to spend. She is careful to strip the argument of superiority, noting that a difference in pace, capacity or preoccupation does not make the other person wrong, it simply places you in different rooms. Three lessons follow, including the point that not everyone will celebrate the improved version of you and that this belongs to their story rather than yours. Energy is framed as a non-renewable asset, a view she attributes to getting older and losing people. The essay ends without a clean resolution to the guilt, recommending quiet gratitude, no dramatic exits and the simple practice of no longer feeding what does not feed you back.
points: Mulder's framing of drift as grief rather than conflict explains why it produces guilt: nothing identifiable went wrong, so the loss feels like a personal failing.
The claim that you cannot grow and pretend at the same time locates the breaking point in the energy cost of shrinking rather than in any decision to leave.
Treating other people's discomfort with your boundaries as belonging to their story rather than yours is her practical remedy for the guilt she admits she has not resolved.
Framing energy as a non-renewable asset, prompted by bereavement and age, gives the boundary argument a basis other than self-interest.
She rejects the dramatic exit entirely, proposing instead that you stop feeding what no longer feeds you and look for rooms where you feel more like yourself.
quotes: Because one of the side effects of growth and coming more into alignment with YOU is that it often comes with quiet grief.
Growth will cost you things that used to feel safe. And that includes relationships that once made perfect sense.
You can’t grow and pretend at the same time. At some point, you stop being able to fake the version of you that someone else prefers.
You start noticing how much effort it takes to shrink yourself. Not out of arrogance, but because your capacity, your perspective, your conversations are different now.
Some people will see your boundaries and ambition as judgment. The insight? That’s about their story, not yours.
If you want to build something meaningful, your energy has to be protected like a non-renewable asset.
Don’t trade your authenticity for approval. Not even in the name of friendship.
